subjects.displayTitle: Expressions of grief, lamentation and sadness
subjects.introduction: Sorrow asks first to be heard. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells a grieving friend to say whatever a troubled heart desires, and he never pretends to stand above grief himself: he writes to his sister of tears he cannot hold back, of a calamity that melted his heart, of hardships falling on his family like spring rain. Bahá’u’lláh’s prayers bring the same honesty before God, who sees the tears and hears the bitter wailing. Grief in the Writings is not scolded away; it is given room, and then it is accompanied. Out of lament rises the counsel of patience, the assurance that death is a door of mercy and that the beloved dead live on, so that mourning opens naturally into prayer for the departed and into the question of the soul’s life beyond this world. Grief also tells the truth about injustice, and so it borders the memory of the martyrs. Finally it becomes practical: visit, listen, provide a livelihood, protect a widow, continue a loved one’s work. There consolation stops being a word and becomes a hand held out.

The reported prayer for release also asks for health if further service remains. How do vulnerability and spiritual purpose coexist? order.why: Longing may arise from exile, distance, delayed correspondence or a journey undertaken in service. Follow the images of Jacob and Joseph into the comparative reading from the Qur’an, where lament and renewed hope occur together. Letters affirm the pain of separation while seeking news, anticipating reunion or explaining a necessary delay. A reported farewell distinguishes bodily distance from spiritual companionship. Read poetic expressions as poetry and personal instructions with their addressees in view. What can remembrance, an honest letter or thoughtful provision accomplish when a meeting is impossible? How might the purpose of a journey change the experience of those who remain?
shortened: O thou who art yearning for the Kingdom!
